# Unveiling the correlations between benzoic acid content, key microbial genera, and metabolites during the storage and transportation of raw yak milk based on multi-omics analysis

**Authors:** Yantao Guo; Yixuan Zhang; Ruiyun Wang; Yiheng Li; Longlin Wang; Chengrui Shi; Xinyun Yu; Jinxiu Ma; Weibing Zhang; Pengjie Wang; Pengcheng Wen

**Affiliations:** aCollege of Food Science and Engineering, Gansu Agricultural University, Lanzhou 730070, China | bGansu Liaoyuan DAIRY CO., LTD, Gannan 747000, China | cDepartment of Nutrition and Health, China Agricultural University, Beijing 100193, China | dQinghai Snowpeak Yak Dairy CO., LTD., Xining 810000, China | eGansu Qimu DAIRY CO., LTD, Jiayuguan 735100, China

## Abstract

Unique transport conditions in Tibetan regions delay the storage of yak milk, particularly during the July–August peak production period at 18 °C, promoting microbial activity and benzoic acid accumulation. This substantially heightens food safety risks associated with consumption. This study used 16S high-throughput sequencing and non-targeted metabolomics to examine the association between benzoic acid content, dominant bacterial genera, and key metabolites. At 0 h of storage (G0), the dominant genera in yak milk were Kaistella, Lactococcus, and Streptococcus. As storage extended to 12 h (G12) and 24 h (G24), Lactococcus emerged as the dominant genus and the key lactic acid bacterium producing endogenous benzoic acid. Metabolomics identified 729 differentially expressed metabolites. Amino acid metabolism is the primary enriched pathway. Myosmine, L-Methionine, L-Phenylalanine, 3-Isochromanone, and Indoline showed strong correlations with Lactococcus. This study provides a theoretical foundation for improving quality control and safety in yak milk production.

## Introduction

Yak milk is known as “natural concentrated milk.”(Wang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024). It represents a significant nutritional resource and economic asset for farmers and herdsmen in the Tibetan Plateau (Wang et al., 2014). Yak milk is rich in conventional nutrients such as protein, fat, and lactose. In addition, it contains a variety of bioactive substances, including immunoglobulins, lactoferrin, and bioactive peptides(Li et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025). Growing recognition of its rich nutritional profile and proven health benefits has led to increasing consumer acceptance. Furthermore, its unique functional properties show considerable potential for developing high-end yak dairy products (Li et al., 2023).

The yak husbandry model in Tibetan regions is characterised by “family-based free-range rearing, traditional grazing practices, and seasonal rotational grazing”(Sapkota et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022). This issue is compounded by local herders' limited educational attainment. Non-standardised milking practices and hygiene conditions, along with temperature fluctuations during raw milk collection, storage, and transport, further contribute to the problem. Together, these factors create conditions conducive to microbial growth and reproduction, which increases the risk of diminished yak milk quality (Machado et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2023). Particularly during the peak milk production period from July to August, when ambient temperatures are elevated (approximately 18 ± 2 °C), and summer pastures are typically distant from processing plants, unstable storage and transportation further accelerate microbial proliferation.

During yak milk procurement, in addition to routine testing for fat and protein content, rapid test strips (with a detection limit of 5–6 μg/mL) are used for preliminary screening of benzoic acid levels, which are often elevated. Precise determination of benzoic acid content necessitates high-performance liquid chromatography. According to the list of food additives stipulated in European Commission Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008, benzoic acid is prohibited in unflavoured dairy products (Jia et al., 2023). However, the benzoic acid detected in yak milk does not originate from artificial addition but primarily results from biotransformation processes mediated by microbial activity. The pathways for benzoic acid formation include the coumaric acid pathway, the phenylalanine pathway, the benzaldehyde pathway, and the hippuric acid pathway. Lactic acid bacteria-mediated conversion of hippuric acid to benzoic acid constitutes the primary source of benzoic acid in yak milk (Allen et al., 2021; Sharma & Ramanathan, 2021). Subsequent processing (e.g., milk powder production) significantly concentrates benzoic acid through dehydration, amplifying product risks. Excessive benzoic acid intake may disrupt key hepatic metabolic pathways, including the urea cycle, gluconeogenesis, fatty acid metabolism, and the tricarboxylic acid cycle (Qi et al., 2009; Saad et al., 2005). When benzoic acid coexists with vitamin C, it may also form benzene precursors (Piper & Piper, 2017), posing particular risks to neonates, children, and individuals with impaired hepatic function who possess weaker metabolic capabilities. Long-term consumption is associated with health risks including asthma, urticaria, cognitive impairment, and metabolic acidosis (Mota et al., 2003; Piper & Piper, 2017). Therefore, systematically elucidating changes in benzoic acid content during yak milk storage and its impact on quality holds significant scientific and practical value.

Combined analysis of microbiome and metabolome data clarifies the link between changes in food quality and microbial communities. It reveals associations between dominant microbes and differentially expressed metabolites(Kumar et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2025). Based on this method, Li et al. (2025) investigated bacterial community dynamics and metabolomic profiles in raw yak milk and cattle-yak milk during refrigeration at 4 °C, followed by the elucidation of interspecific differences in milk storage. Liang et al. (2025) employed 16S rRNA gene high-throughput sequencing and non-targeted metabolomics to identify core functional microbial communities and their metabolic pathways involved in Qula fermentation.

Most research has focused on refrigeration at 4 °C. This study examines how yak milk changes at typical milking-season temperatures (18 ± 2 °C). By tracking endogenous benzoic acid, it addresses a gap in understanding practical storage and transportation. This study explains changes in benzoic acid levels and other physicochemical indicators over storage and transport. It also analyzes the shift in microbial community structure during storage and identifies key bacterial genera. The study profiles metabolites in raw yak milk and shows how the overall metabolome changes over time, screening for significant differences. Finally, it connects microbiome and metabolomics data, revealing how benzoic acid content relates to dominant bacteria and metabolites.

## Materials and methods

### Chemical reagents

Acetonitrile, methanol (chromatographic purity) Shandong Keyuan Biochemical Co., Ltd.; Ammonium acetate Shandong Keyuan Biochemical Co., Ltd.; Benzoic acid standard (CAS: 65–85-0, purity ≥99.9%) Tanmo Quality Inspection Standard Substance Centre; Hippuric acid standard (CAS: 495–69-2, purity ≥98%) Shanghai Yuanye Biotechnology Co., Ltd.; Methyl tertiary-butyl ether Beijing Wokai Biotechnology Co., Ltd.; Agarose Gel Reagent Agarose, Agarose Gel Electrophoresis Buffer Row Liquid TAE Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA; Marker Bao Bioengineering (Dalian) Co.

### Collection of yak milk samples

The yak raw milk used in this trial was supplied by a family farm, located in Oula Town, Maqu County, Gannan Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Gansu Province, China. Yaks are managed under a traditional, fully pasture-based system without supplementary feeding, having unrestricted access to forage and water sources. Raw yak milk is collected through manual milking by herders, then filtered through disposable gauze into sterile cryogenic tubes. Each tube contained 100 mL, with a total of 18 tubes collected and randomly divided into three groups (n = 6). Samples are immediately preserved in dry ice and transported to the Key Laboratory of Dairy Biotechnology and Engineering at Gansu Agricultural University. Upon arrival at the laboratory, one batch of samples was randomly selected as the 0-h sample and stored directly in a − 80 °C freezer. The remaining two batches were thawed and stored at 18 °C for 12 h and 24 h respectively. At the conclusion of each time point, six samples from the corresponding batch were immediately transferred to the −80 °C freezer for cryopreservation, to be used for subsequent parameter determination.

### Physicochemical parameters

A pH meter (PHS-3E, Remco, China) was used for pH determination in the test; the determination of titratable acid content was completed by the phenolphthalein indicator method with reference to GB 5009.239–2016, “National Standard for Food Safety, Determination of Acidity of Foodstuffs”.

### Determination of benzoic acid and hippuric acid content

Referring to the national standard GB 5009.28–2016 “Determination of Benzoic Acid, Sorbic Acid and Saccharin Sodium in Foods of National Standards for Food Safety”, the first method of liquid chromatography, through the optimisation of the sample pre-treatment conditions, liquid chromatography analysis conditions(So et al., 2023), 2 mL of yak milk samples were taken in a 10 mL centrifuge tube, followed by the addition of 6 mL of methanol, vortex mixing with a vortex mixer (DC12V-1 A, Qilinbel, China), ultrasonic cleaning machine (KQ-250B, Kunshan Ultrasonics, China) for 30 min, and freezing in a refrigerator (BCD-518WLHSSE5D9U1, Haier, China) at −20 °C for 30 min, 12000 r-min-1 Centrifugation was performed for 10 min, and 1 mL of the supernatant was taken and filtered through 0.22 μm filter membrane into the sample bottle for analysis. High-performance liquid chromatograph (LC-20, Shimadzu, Japan) column: model C18 (4.6 mm*150 mm, 5 μm). Mobile phase: ammonium acetate (0.02 mol/L): acetonitrile = 90:10 (V/V), flow rate: 1 mL/min; injection volume: 10 μL; column temperature: 25 °C; detection wavelength: 230 nm.

### Sequencing of 16S amplicons from yak milk at different storage time points

The method of Li et al. (2025) was referenced with minor modifications. Yak milk samples (n = 6; 1 mL each) were centrifuged at 13,000 ×g for 20 min at 4 °C. After removing the lipid layer with a sterile swab, nucleic acids were extracted from the precipitate using the OMEGA Soil DNA Kit (M5635–02). The extracted DNA was assessed by 0.8% agarose gel electrophoresis for size verification and quantified using a Nanodrop spectrophotometer. The bacterial 16S rRNA V3-V4 region was subsequently amplified with barcoded primers 338F (5’-ACTCCTACGGGGAGGCAGCA-3′) and 806R (5’-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3′). PCR amplification was conducted under the following conditions: initial denaturation at 98 °C for 5 min; followed by 25 cycles of denaturation at 98 °C for 30 s, primer annealing at 52 °C for 30 s, and extension at 72 °C for 45 s; with a final extension at 72 °C for 5 min. The amplified products were then held at 12 °C for storage. Paired-end sequencing (2 × 250 bp) was conducted on an Illumina NovaSeq platform with the NovaSeq 6000 SP Reagent Kit (500 cycles). Microbiome bioinformatics were processed in QIIME2 (version 2019.4), following a modified official tutorial. Raw sequences were demultiplexed with the demux plugin, followed by primer removal using cutadapt. Subsequent quality control, including filtering, denoising, merging, and chimera removal, was performed with the DADA2 plugin. High-quality sequences from each sample were clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs) at 97% similarity using either the QIIME2 DADA2 workflow or Vsearch. Finally, alpha diversity was evaluated based on OTU distribution across samples, with sequencing depth adequacy confirmed by rarefaction curves.

### Untargeted metabolomics analysis of yak milk with different storage times

Referring to the method of Khamis et al. (2017), the milk samples were thawed, vortexed, and mixed for 1 min at 4 °C. An appropriate amount of the sample was pipetted into a 2 mL centrifuge tube, 200 μL of methanol and 200 μL of Methyl Tertiary Butyl Ether were added, and vortexed for 1 min. Then, centrifugation (12,000 rpm, 4 °C, 15 min) was performed to collect the supernatant, and filtered through a 0.22 μm membrane. Finally, the filtrate was added to the detection vial for LC-MS/MS detection.

Chromatographic separation was performed on a Thermo Vanquish UHPLC system equipped with an ACQUITY UPLC® HSS T3 column (2.1 × 100 mm, 1.8 μm). The column temperature was maintained at 40 °C, and the injection volume was 2 μL. A mobile phase consisting of (A2) 0.1% formic acid in water and (B2) 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile was used at a flow rate of 0.3 mL/min under the following gradient program: 0–1 min, 10% B2; 1–5 min, 10%–98% B2; 5–6.5 min, 98% B2; 6.5–6.6 min, 98%–10% B2; 6.6–8 min, 10% B2.For negative ion mode, the mobile phases consisted of 5 mM ammonium formate in water (A3) and acetonitrile (B3), with the following gradient: 0–1 min, 10% B3; 1–5 min, 10%–98% B3; 5–6.5 min, 98% B3; 6.5–6.6 min, 98%–10% B3; 6.6–8 min, 10% B3. Mass spectrometry was performed on a Thermo Orbitrap Exploris 120 instrument equipped with an electrospray ion source (ESI), acquiring data in both positive and negative modes. Key MS parameters were set as follows: spray voltage, 3.50 kV (positive) and − 2.50 kV (negative); sheath gas, 40 arb; auxiliary gas, 10 arb; capillary temperature, 325 °C. Full MS scans (resolution: 60,000) covered a range of m/z 100–1000. Data-dependent MS/MS acquisition involved fragmenting the top 4 ions using HCD (collision energy: 30%; resolution: 15,000), with dynamic exclusion enabled to reduce redundant fragmentation (Want et al., 2013).

Raw mass spectrometry data were converted to mzXML format using MSConvert (Proteowizard v3.0.8789) (Rasmussen et al., 2022). Peak detection, filtering, and alignment were subsequently performed using the R XCMS package (v3.12.0). The analysis used the following parameters: bw = 2, ppm = 15, peakwidth = c(5,30), mzwid = 0.015, mzdiff = 0.01, with the “centWave” method. This process yielded a quantified metabolite list. Data were then corrected by total peak area normalization. Metabolites were identified by searching against public databases (HMD, Massbank, LipidMaps, mzCloud, KEGG) and a self-built standard library (Nomimetabolism), with a mass tolerance of <30 ppm. Further confirmation was achieved by matching MS/MS spectra against database fragmentation patterns.

### Statistical analyses

Multivariate statistical analyses, including PCA and OPLS-DA, were performed using the Rropls package. The OPLS-DA model was used to calculate VIP values. Subsequently, metabolic pathway analysis was conducted by referencing the KEGG database. All statistical analyses and graphing were performed using GraphPad Prism 9.0.

Each sample was measured in six replicates, with results expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Statistical analysis of the experimental data was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics 28.0. Intergroup differences were assessed using permutation analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) based on distance matrices generated with the vegan package. Differences in α-diversity and chemical composition were evaluated using the Kruskal-Wallis test or a one-way ANOVA. Differentially expressed metabolites were screened using Student's t-tests and Wilcoxon tests. Hypergeometric distribution tests assessed the significance of metabolic pathway enrichment. Different lowercase letters denote significant differences (P < 0.05). Network analysis between metabolites and microorganisms was conducted using the Mantel test based on Spearman's correlation coefficients. Data visualisations were subsequently generated using Cloud Tools (https://www.biodeep.cn) and Cytoscape 3.10.3 software.

## Results and analyses

### Changes in pH and titratable acid (TA), benzoic acid, and hippuric acid content during storage of yak milk

Changes in pH and TA reflect the acid-producing capacity of microorganisms, which have an important influence on the stability of yak milk quality, shelf life, and food safety. As shown in Table 1, significant differences were observed in the dynamic changes in pH, TA, benzoic acid, and hippuric acid during yak milk storage (p < 0.05). During storage, the pH and hippuric acid decreased, while TA and benzoic acid increased. The pH of yak milk decreased from 6.55 at the beginning to 6.13. During storage, the TA increased significantly from 16 to 26.7 (p < 0.05), and it was clear that the yak milk at storage site G24 had deteriorated, as indicated by the pH and TA values. ### Analysis of yak milk microbial community structure and function

To comprehensively evaluate microbial community structure, this study employed multidimensional estimates of alpha diversity. Cover was represented by Good's cover index, richness by Chao's 1 and observed species indices, diversity by Shannon and Simpson indices, evolutionarily based diversity by Faith's PD index, and evenness by Pielou's evenness index. Results are presented in Fig. 1A, showing that all samples exhibited excellent coverage exceeding 99%, indicating detection of the majority of bacterial systems. Based on the Chao1 index and observed species index, the G12 sample exhibited higher richness than the other samples. The G12 sample also showed higher Shannon, Simpson, and Pielou's evenness indices, indicating greater diversity and evenness than the other two samples. Changes in microbial population and species during storage of yak milk are key factors affecting its quality and safety. To investigate the evolution of microbial communities during yak milk storage, OTU labels were taxonomically analysed at both the phylum and genus levels in this study. Fig. 1B shows that four major bacterial phyla were identified in yak milk samples across three storage stages: Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria, and Actinobacteria. Together, these four phyla accounted for more than 99% of the total bacterial community of the samples, constituting the core microbial composition during yak milk storage. According to the heat map of microbial composition at the genus level (Fig. 1D), the bacterial community structure undergoes significant succession during yak milk storage (p < 0.05). The initially dominant genera are gradually replaced, and the originally non-dominant genera become dominant taxa, with G12 being the key turning point of this transition. Specifically, as shown in Fig. 1C, Kaistella dominated in the 0 h storage samples. From 12 h onwards, Lactococcus became more dominant, with significantly higher levels in the 12 h and 24 h samples than in the 0 h samples (p < 0.05). In addition, Streptococcus and Leuconostoc were detected in some samples. Lactococcus, Streptococcus, and Leuconostoc were the dominant genera during storage, all belonging to the Firmicutes. Notably, genera associated with foodborne pathogenicity and environmental contamination were also detected in some samples, including Acinetobacter, Enterobacteriaceae_A, and Chryseobacterium, suggesting a possible microbiological contamination risk during hygiene or processing.

The results of the LDA Effect Size (LEfSe) are shown in Fig. 1F. The absolute value of the LDA score represents the magnitude of the effect of different storage times, with an LDA score greater than 4 set as the threshold for identifying biomarkers. Bacteria from 6 orders, 7 families, and 8 genera showed significantdifferences in abundance (p < 0.05). The biomarker genera were Lactococcus_A in group G0, and Kaistella, Streptococcus, Acidovorax_A, Ottowia, Dokdonella_A, Pseudoclavibacter_A, and Chryseobacterium in group G24. The microbial populations were mainly focused on primary functional metabolism, including carbohydrate, amino acid, cofactor, and vitamin metabolism, in the functional prediction (Fig. 1E).

### Analysis of metabolite composition of yak milk at different storage times

To further investigate how yak milk metabolomics changes over time, a comprehensive metabolomic profile was conducted using LC-MS/MS. PCA was used to highlight trends in the overall distribution of metabolomics data and the degree of variation between sample groups. As seen in Fig. 2 (A, D), the variance contribution of PC1 in positive ion mode was 42.9%, and that of PC2 was 21.3%. The variance contributions of PC1 and PC2 in negative ion mode are 33% and 19.4%, respectively. It is clear from the principal component plots that there were large differences between the sample groups across storage times. To better reflect the differences between groups, the OPLS-DA method in supervised mode was applied. The OPLS-DA model in both positive and negative ion modes could significantly cluster and separate G0, G12, and G24 (p < 0.05) (Fig. 2B, E). The results of both OPLS-DA and PCA indicated that these three sample sets could be significantly separated (p < 0.05), suggesting that the metabolite differences among them were obvious. This suggests that the metabolite differences were influenced by the storage time of yak milk. To guard against overfitting, we performed a permutation test. The model's R2 and Q2 values all surpassed 0.5 in both ion modes (Fig. 2C, F). These results indicate good predictability and reproducibility. We initially extracted 22,478 MS features using XCMS in R from both ion modes. Significant differential metabolites were identified using statistical testing, with screening based on P-values and VIPs (p < 0.05). The number of differential metabolites up- and down-regulated in positive and negative ion modes is shown in Fig. 2 (G, I). The Venn diagrams in positive and negative ion modes (Fig. 2H, J) clearly demonstrate the distribution of differential metabolites among the three comparison groups. A total of 1369 differentially expressed metabolites were shared in the positive ion mode, while 1096 were shared in the negative ion mode (Table S1).

To better illustrate the distribution of differentially expressed metabolites in secondary mass spectrometry, a volcano plot was generated to visualise metabolites measured across three developmental stages. Setting thresholds at VIP > 1.0, P < 0.05, and FC ≥ 2 or FC ≤ 0.5, a total of 729 differentially expressed metabolites were identified, categorised as shown in Fig. 4A. Comparisons between G12 vs G0, G24 vs G0, and G24 vs G12 yielded 36, 10, and 35 unique differentially expressed metabolites respectively, with 40 metabolites common across all three comparisons (Fig. 3E). Heatmap analysis (Fig. 3F) clearly revealed markedly distinct metabolic profiles among the three sample groups. As indicated by the colour scale, distinct clusters of red (high expression) and blue (low expression) regions emerged across the three sample groups, as depicted in Fig. 3D. The G12 vs G0, G24 vs G12, and G24 vs G0 comparisons yielded 242, 291, and 328 differentially expressed metabolites, respectively. These were predominantly concentrated in organic acids and their derivatives, amino acids and their derivatives, alkaloids, ketones and their derivatives, and alcohols and their derivatives (Fig. 4C, E, G). ### Association analysis of genus-level bacteria with differential metabolites in yak milk

There is a mutual influence and interaction between microorganisms and metabolites. The metabolites with top 50 VIP values among the differential metabolites were selected for Pearson correlation analysis with the results of microbial communities (genus level), and the results are shown in Fig. 5. In the microbial-metabolism relationship, Lactococcus_A, Enterobacteriaceae_A, Leuconostoc_B, and Streptococcaceae showed a significant positive correlation with Myosmine, L-Methionine, L-Phenylalanine, 3-Isochromanone, and Indoline, and a significant negative correlation with the other differential metabolites were significantly negatively correlated (p < 0.05). In contrast, changes in abundance of Kaistella, Moraxellaceae, Chryseobacterium, and Acinetobacter were significantly negatively correlated with the aforementioned metabolite association patterns and positively correlated with the remaining metabolites (p < 0.05). ## Discussion

Yak milk faces significant storage and transportation challenges during peak lactation periods. In Tibetan regions, average temperatures during this period reach 18 °C. Environmental conditions, coupled with a lack of large-scale refrigeration facilities, result in delays in storage and transport. During this process, dynamic changes in microbial communities exert multifaceted negative impacts on the quality of yak milk and its products (Li et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025). The sources of microbial contamination in yak milk are complex. They include microorganisms from the yak's surface, the milking environment, and feeding conditions. Additionally, contamination arises from storage containers and human handling. This study examines changes in benzoic acid levels alongside microbial communities and metabolism at different storage and transport time points, exploring the interrelationships among benzoic acid, microorganisms, and their metabolites, as illustrated in Fig. 6A.Fig. 6Schematic diagram of the process and mechanism of material and microbiological changes in yak milk storage process. Using 16S amplicon sequencing, significant temporal changes in the microbial community structure of yak milk were observed (p < 0.05). Under storage and transportation at 18 °C, microbial richness, diversity, and evenness peaked at the 12 h sample. This time point marked a critical turning point in microbial community succession during storage and transportation. As microbial metabolism consumed oxygen, the system gradually shifted from microaerophilic to anaerobic conditions. As a result, lactic acid bacteria, mainly facultative anaerobes, thrived under low oxygen, while aerobic or strictly aerobic bacteria experienced growth inhibition. In G0 samples, Kaistella, Lactococcus, and Streptococcus were dominant (about 60% combined). In G12 and G24 samples, Lactococcus increased to about 42% and 68%, becoming dominant. Notably, the genus Lactococcus is widely present in raw milk (Vahabzadeh & Özpinar, 2018; Yerlikaya, 2019). The predominant bacteria in raw buffalo milk before storage for 24 h are also Lactococcus and Streptococcus (Li et al., 2016). Furthermore, stored yak milk samples exhibited pronounced psychrophilic characteristics, with psychrophilic bacteria accounting for over 80% of the abundance. This group included Lactococcus, Kaistella, Streptococcus, and Leuconostoc, all of which are frequently detected in raw milk (von Neubeck et al., 2015).

During storage of yak milk, lactobacilli proliferate rapidly and break down lactose into glucose and galactose, which are further metabolized into organic acids, predominantly lactic acid (Li et al., 2022). This process increases acidity and lowers pH in yak milk. The increased acidity partially inhibits Kaistella growth, which may explain why this genus fails to maintain a dominant position in yak milk. Concurrently, we observed a 1:1 correlation between changes in benzoic acid and hippuric acid levels at different storage time points. Given prior reports that lactic acid bacteria can convert hippuric acid to benzoic acid at a 1:1 conversion rate (Yerlikaya et al., 2021), and that microbiome analysis in this study revealed a significant increase in Lactococcus (a lactic acid bacterium) abundance, our data strongly suggest Lactobacillus as the key mediator (p < 0.05). Furthermore, benzoic acid accumulation exerts additional selective effects on the microbial community. Benzoic acid effectively inhibits the growth of yeasts, molds, and most bacteria, but its inhibitory effect on lactic acid bacteria is negligible (Yerlikaya et al., 2021). This aligns with our observations: as storage time increased and benzoic acid levels rose, the relative abundance of Streptococcus and Lactococcus increased, while the abundance of other microbial groups decreased.

The dynamic succession of microbial communities in yak milk is a key factor driving the continuous evolution of its metabolome. Lactococcus, Streptococcus, and Leuconostoc, identified at different storage and transportation time points in yak milk, are dominant genera in dairy products and primarily belong to the phylum Firmicutes. These bacteria produce short peptides, free amino acids, and short-chain fatty acids by metabolizing lactose and other carbohydrates, as well as proteins, peptides, and fats (Anastasiou et al., 2022). Protein degradation, lipid degradation, carbohydrate utilization, and acid accumulation negatively impact the nutritional value, flavor, and sensory quality of yak milk and subsequent dairy products (Xiong et al., 2024). For instance, protein degradation produces bitterness, lipid degradation yields a soapy flavor, and acid accumulation leads to rancidity and impairs yak milk curdling (Li et al., 2025). Further studies reveal that microbially generated branched acids integrate amino acid metabolism, alkaloid biosynthesis, hormone synthesis, and carbohydrate metabolism, acting as pivotal nodes that regulate metabolite flux (Fig. 6B). Branched acids generate tyrosine via prebenzoic acid and 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid, with tyrosine serving as a precursor for thyroid hormone synthesis (Mao et al., 2017; Marechal et al., 2022). Tryptophan can generate tryptamine, o-aminobenzoate, and indoleacetic acid via the indole and phenylethylamine pathways, with o-aminobenzoate participating in the synthesis of quinoline alkaloids (Shan et al., 2023). The acylated forms of CoA (acetyl-CoA and lipoyl-CoA, etc.) directly or indirectly participate in carbohydrate synthesis and metabolism. In this process, the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, glycolysis, and the methylenepyruvate phosphate (MEP) pathway may be essential for energy and material conversion (Hu et al., 2025; Shan et al., 2023). Furthermore, intermediates from these biological processes may be released or further metabolized to aldehydes, ketones, alcohols, esters, phenols, and organic acids via β-oxidation, the lipoxygenase (LOX) pathway, and glycoside hydrolysis (Xiao et al., 2022; Xiao et al., 2024). In summary, our study elucidates the potential mechanisms underlying metabolic transformations in raw yak milk during storage, providing a scientific basis for advancing the understanding of yak milk storage quality.

During storage and transportation of raw yak milk, metabolite accumulation primarily results from microbial activity, with certain metabolites serving as markers of dairy spoilage (Machado et al., 2017). These spoilage markers exhibit a sustained increase in concentration throughout storage and transport, demonstrating a significant positive correlation with microbial growth (Jia et al., 2019; Parlapani et al., 2017). This study identified Myosmine, L-Methionine, L-Phenylalanine, 3-Isochromanone, and Indoline as being closely associated with spoilage-related microbial communities. These metabolites were initially absent or present in very low quantities, but their levels gradually increased with extended storage and transport duration. The rise in metabolite content showed good correlation with microbial growth. Consequently, the aforementioned metabolites hold promise as markers of yak milk spoilage.

## Conclusion

This study systematically analysed the dynamic changes in microorganisms and metabolites in yak milk during storage and transportation at 18 ± 2 °C by integrating 16S amplicon sequencing with non-targeted metabolomics. By elucidating alterations in microbial community structure and metabolite profiles, we have deepened our multifaceted understanding of the fundamental mechanisms underlying yak milk storage and spoilage. Findings indicate that dominant bacterial genera in yak milk shifted from Kaistella to Lactococcus with prolonged storage and transport, with the latter confirmed as the key microorganism driving endogenous benzoic acid production. Metabolomic analysis further revealed amino acid metabolism as a core active pathway during storage and transport, identifying five metabolite biomarkers highly correlated with quality changes. These biomarkers serve as valuable targets for real-time quality monitoring and early detection of spoilage events. These insights hold significant implications for developing targeted preservation strategies and quality control measures aimed at enhancing the safety and shelf life of high-altitude specialty milk and its derivatives, particularly in regions where such products are crucial to cultural heritage and economic livelihoods.
